subject: gramophone
pitch: An antique gramophone on a carved walnut cabinet. A huge flaring brass horn shaped like a morning-glory flower, a black record with a red label on the turntable, a silver tonearm, a wind-up crank on the side and little claw feet. The brass has a warm, slightly green patina, and the wood is inlaid with a pale floral pattern.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the gramophone model's dimensions and layout—sizing the cabinet, horn, and tone arm proportions in meters before building the three.js scene.

For the cabinet itself, I'm raising it on four brass claw feet, placing the turntable on top, and giving the wood surfaces a floral-inlay canvas texture for decorative detail.

For the mechanical parts, I'm positioning a brass turntable platter with a black record and red label, then building the tonearm as a pivoting group with a cylinder arm angled from a base pivot to a head shell above the record, plus a horn shape built from a lathe profile that flares outward and upward like a morning glory.

Since standard lathe geometry is radially symmetric, I need a custom buffer geometry approach to scallop the horn's mouth edge — computing radius as a function of both position along the horn and angle around it, adding lobed variation near the flared end to get the wavy scalloped lip, then computing vertex normals and orienting the whole horn so its throat meets the tonearm.

Shaping the horn's radius profile with scalloped petal-like ridges near the mouth, then adding a rim detail at the mouth edge for finishing detail.

I'm also working out the gooseneck connecting the cabinet to the horn throat using a tapered brass cylinder, and computing the horn's direction vector and quaternion rotation so the mouth flares forward and upward past the cabinet front at the right height and depth.

Now I'm placing the hand crank on the right side of the cabinet—a brass disc housing with a rod and knob sphere bent outward—and adding the four claw feet as short cylindrical legs positioned at each corner beneath the cabinet.

For the claws themselves, I'm building each as a small sphere resting on the floor with three splayed talons rendered as thin cones pointing downward and outward, giving the grip-and-ball look. I'm also sketching a brass trim strip along the cabinet's top edge plus corner caps, and settling on walnut (#5a3a22) for the wood and a brass tone (#b5894a) with a canvas-based patina texture for the metal accents.

I'm now fleshing out the brass texture with gold base and random green patina splotches, making sure UVs are defined properly across both the lathed and custom geometry so the texture maps correctly. For the other materials I'm setting record black (#111) with low roughness, a red label with a thin gold ring accent, and silver at full metalness with moderate roughness.

For the wood grain, I'm drawing a brown base with sine-wave streaks for grain and adding a repeating pale floral inlay pattern using light tan ellipses (#e8d9b5), plus considering a couple of thin pale inlay bands along the front face for extra detail, though I want to keep the added geometry minimal.

Now I'm seeding the RNG and working out the turntable assembly's geometry — placing the pivot, tonearm, horn throat, turntable disc, and record precisely relative to the cabinet's top surface so nothing collides or clips, defining a helper to draw cylinders between two points for the tonearm, and checking that the horn throat position stays within the cabinet's depth bounds.

I'm designing a parametric horn geometry function that builds a widening cone with a morning-glory flare, using a power curve for the radius growth and a scalloped petal effect (controlled by a lobe count) so the mouth has a fluted, flower-like rim rather than a plain circle.

I'm figuring out vertex positions and UVs across rings and segments, planning a seam duplication so texture coordinates wrap cleanly, and deciding to let computeVertexNormals handle shading even with a minor seam artifact there. For sizing, I'm settling on a 0.27 mouth radius with 10 lobes at 64 segments and 40 rings for a reasonable vertex count, and I'm adding a thin rim torus at the mouth opening using the brass material with double-sided rendering so the interior doesn't look hollow from outside angles.

Now I'm orienting the horn as a group along a direction vector using a quaternion rotation from the Y axis, then positioning it at the throat point, while separately grouping each claw foot. For the crank mechanism, I'm placing a cylindrical housing on the cabinet's side face, adding a shaft and arm extending outward, and topping it with a small handle sphere, all in brass.

I'm now laying out the cabinet body as a box centered above the feet, with the feet filling the gap between the floor and the box bottom, and I'm starting to add a brass trim strip around the top perimeter using thin boxes.

I decide to add the front and side perimeter trim pieces for the cabinet top, skip a separate plinth lid, and move to texturing the cabinet surfaces with a canvas-based wood grain pattern including floral inlay motifs, plus a brass texture with patina blotches and highlights for the decorative hardware.

Writing the random number generator and canvas texture helpers...

Building 3D helper functions for connecting cylinders between points, then designing the claw foot geometry with a leg, ball joint, and three outward-pointing talons for the cabinet base.

Working out the tonearm geometry now—placing the pivot column and head positions, then running the arm from pivot to headshell with a small counterweight sphere on the back end, plus a disc base for the pivot mount on the cabinet top.

Now I'm positioning the turntable platter, mat, and record stack so they sit at the right heights relative to the cabinet top, with the record and label slightly overlapping the platter for a natural fit.

I'm adding a silver spindle through the center, then layering a few thin dark-gray rings on the record surface to simulate grooves using flat ring geometries rotated to face upward. Finally I'm starting to lay out the horn group, positioning its throat just above the cabinet top near the back.

Now I'm computing the horn's mouth position by extending the throat point along a direction vector, then adding a brass reproducer housing at the throat as a small cylinder, plus a rim torus and collar as child meshes of the horn group. I'm also planning brass trim strips along the cabinet's top edges, placing the crank housing on the left side, and starting to add pale inlay bands on the front face.

Writing horn geometry function...

Finishing the geometry setup and considering normal winding — since I'm using DoubleSide materials for brass, Three.js handles back-face normal flipping automatically, so the horn's interior/exterior lighting should work correctly either way.

Now defining the material palette: walnut with a canvas wood texture, brass with a metal texture and high metalness, plus flat PBR values for silver, black, red, pale ivory, and groove accents. I'm settling on final petal shaping with the mouth scallop at 12% and the rim torus sized to match the flared horn opening, then moving to write out the complete scene code with the page's meta description.
